title: Climate Change and Yellow Fever in South America: Ecological Factors, Emerging Risks and Future Transmission Scenarios
content: Yellow fever (YF) remains a major public health threat in South America, where transmission is closely linked to climatic conditions, forest ecosystems, sylvatic mosquito vectors, and non-human primates. Climate change, together with deforestation, biodiversity loss, and expanding human activities, is reshaping the ecological interactions that sustain yellow fever virus (YFV) circulation. This narrative review examines how climatic and environmental changes influence YF epidemiology, emerging transmission risks, and potential future scenarios in South America. Increasing temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, humidity changes, and extreme weather events may affect mosquito abundance, survival, vector competence, and geographic distribution. At the same time, forest fragmentation, agricultural expansion, mining, and urbanization modify interactions among vectors, non-human primates, and human populations, potentially increasing spillover opportunities. Recent outbreaks in Brazil, Colombia, and other South American countries underscore the continued vulnerability of populations living near forest ecosystems, particularly where vaccination coverage remains insufficient. Future climate scenarios suggest possible shifts in transmission seasonality, expansion into previously less receptive geographical areas, and increased exposure at forest–urban interfaces. Although sustained urban transmission has not been documented for decades, the widespread presence of Aedes aegypti warrants continued vigilance. Addressing these challenges requires integrated One Health strategies combining climate-informed surveillance, monitoring of non-human primate epizootics, ecological modeling, targeted vaccination, ecosystem conservation, and regional cooperation. Strengthening these approaches is essential to anticipate emerging risks and prevent future YF outbreaks in South America.
